extracted.intended_audience: geologists, natural philosophers, and students of geognosy (19th-century field and laboratory observers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and observational standards for identifying, classifying, and inferring the origin and metamorphic history of rocks (eruptive/plutonic vs volcanic, sedimentary, and metamorphic) from field and experimental evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal groups of endogenous/erupted rocks
rubrics_metrics.description: The erupted (endogenous) or compact rocks are classifiable into principal groups such as granite and syenite, quartzose porphyry, greenstones/diorite, hypersthene rock, euphotide/serpentine, melaphyre, basalt, phonolite, trachyte, and colerite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These groups are enumerated as the immediate products of terrestrial activity; each has characteristic mineralogy and field relations (e.g., granite often traverses syenite in veins). Examples and localities are cited throughout the text to illustrate each group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field indicators of granite formation and relative age
rubrics_metrics.description: Granite frequently appears more recent than syenite (often traversing it in veins) and displays surface features such as a crust cleft into blocks, tabular divisions, concentric scaling, hemispherical eminences, and flattened spherical masses divided into concentric layers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational examples: Hartz district, Mysore, Lower Peru, Lake Kolivan, Las Trincheras, Irtysch valley; these morphological features (scales, ledges, concentric layers) are diagnostic field signs of granite emplacement and subsequent contraction or expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartzose porphyry characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Quartzose porphyry commonly occurs as veins; its base is generally a finely granular mixture of the same elements as the larger embedded crystals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In granitic porphyry poor in quartz, the feldspathic base appears granular and laminated. Use mineral texture and vein relationships to identify quartzose porphyry in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greenstones and diorite identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Greenstones and diorite are granular mixtures of white albite and blackish-green hornblende, sometimes forming dioritic porphyry when crystals are set in a denser base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They may occur as strata, veins, or globular masses resembling basaltic domes, and may pass into serpentine or enclose diallage laminae (examples: Fichtelgebirge). Note textural and mineralogical transitions to infer origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basalt, phonolite, and trachyte lamination and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Basalt often contains olivine and constituents dissolvable by acids; phonolite and trachyte are frequently divided into thin laminae, giving them an appearance of stratification over large extents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mesotype and nepheline can be important constituents of basalt; nepheline presence links basalt to other pyroxenic rocks. Lamination and mineralogy inform on emplacement and subsequent weathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedimentary strata categories and origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Sedimentary strata include schist (lower/upper transition rocks including Silurian and Devonian), carboniferous deposits, limestones (zechstein, muschelkalk, Jura, chalk), travertine and freshwater limestones, and infusorial deposits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between strata formed by precipitation (chemical solution) and deposition (suspended detritus). These distinctions matter for interpretations of fossil envelopment and paleoenvironmental conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between precipitated and deposited sediments
rubrics_metrics.description: Sediments may be precipitated (chemically dissolved then solidified, e.g., some limestones) or deposited (suspended and mechanically accumulated, e.g., sandstones and conglomerates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction affects the understanding of how organic bodies become enveloped (petrification) and the chemical history of the strata; observe particle size, texture, and geochemical context to infer mode of formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamorphism: causes and diagnostic outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Endogenous (erupted) rocks exert elevating and disturbing influences and may change the chemical composition and internal structure of surrounding strata, producing new rocks such as gneiss, mica slate, and granular limestone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metamorphism is not solely a contact phenomenon: it comprises all generic phenomena accompanying the appearance of an erupted mass (thermal influence, vapors, pressure, time). Look for transformed lithology, recrystallization, and loss or preservation of fossils (e.g., belemnites) as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plutonic versus volcanic emplacement characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Plutonic rocks (granite, porphyry, serpentine) were likely protruded in a softened condition from long, widely-extending gorges and occur in extended masses; volcanic rocks (trachyte, basalt, lava) appear as band-like streams, often issuing from narrow fissures or slender threads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use morphology (extended masses vs flows), presence of veins, craterless domes, or columnar structures to distinguish plutonic from volcanic origin. Examples of narrow basaltic effusion vs large plutonic masses are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooling rate controls on texture and crystallinity
rubrics_metrics.description: The cooling rate and pressure under which volcanic masses were fused determine their products: rapid cooling yields a black glass with homogeneous fracture; slow cooling yields a stony, granular crystalline structure with crystals formed in cavities or enclosed in the matrix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental and field observations (e.g., diorite, augitic porphyry, basalt, Etna lava) should inform interpretations of cooling history from observed textures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of pressure and crystallization method on carbonate products
rubrics_metrics.description: Carbonate of lime fused under great pressure retains its carbonic acid and cools into granular limestone; crystallization by the dry method yields saccharoidal marble; the humid method produces calcareous spar and aragonite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply laboratory fusion/pressure results to explain natural occurrences of granular limestone, saccharoidal marble, calcareous spar, and aragonite in contact-affected terrains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature-dependent crystal form and dimorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences of temperature modify the direction in which particles arrange during crystallization and affect crystal form; some substances (e.g., sulphur) exhibit dimorphism depending on temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider thermal gradients and experimental mineralogy (Mitscherlich) when interpreting mineral habits and polymorphs in metamorphic or igneous contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact metamorphism diagnostic: intersecting divisional planes
rubrics_metrics.description: Schist converted by proximity to Plutonic rocks may show a new system of divisional planes intersecting the original stratification at near right angles, indicating a subsequent metamorphic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation of dual plane systems in altered schist indicates metamorphic overprinting; see Elie de Beaumont and others for documented examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silicification as indicator of Plutonic contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Penetration of silica can traverse argillaceous schist with quartz, transforming it into whetstone or silicious schist; extreme silicification produces ribbon jasper associated with contact by augitic porphyry, dioritic porphyry, or hypersthenic rock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate silica-rich veins, ribbon jasper, and associated porphyritic intrusions (examples: Orsk, Aufschkul, Bogoslowsk, Elba, Tuscany) as evidence of contact metamorphic silicification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation of compact limestone into granular limestone or marble
rubrics_metrics.description: Compact limestones may be converted into granular limestone (Carrara, Parian marbles) or saccharoidal marble by the action of adjacent Plutonic rocks, sometimes via intermediate gneiss or mica slate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess purity of adjacent schists (mica content, argillaceous content) to predict the crystalline quality of resulting marble; field examples include Carrara, Paros, and regions in the Pyrenees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation of limestone into dolomite and its signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Masses of dolomite (e.g., Southern Tyrol) represent metamorphism by massive eruptive rocks: the formation includes fissures, cavities lined with rhomboidal magnesian spar, talc laminae, serpentine masses, and loss of stratification and fossils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dolomitization may occur simultaneously with eruption through fissures filled with vapors rather than by direct contact alone; search for mineral assemblages and textural loss of fossils as diagnostic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penumbra effect: limited depth of contact metamorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Erupted rock does not always transform adjacent strata to great depth—sometimes only a slight transformation or 'penumbra' occurs (example: basalt veins traversing chalk at Belfast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate degree and depth of alteration near contacts; limited transformation implies restricted thermal/chemical influence or rapid cooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference rule from consistent associations
rubrics_metrics.description: When two phenomena are repeatedly associated (e.g., melaphyre occurrence and transformation of compact limestone), their frequent co-occurrence justifies causal inference; absence of one when the other is present may mean missing attendant conditions rather than refutation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated observational associations across wide regions to form hypotheses about causality, but consider the possibility of absent conditions or channels conveying Plutonic influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological standard: combine observation with chemical experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of metamorphism was established by step-by-step observation of individual phases and direct chemical experiments on fusion points, pressure, and cooling times to support inductive conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate meticulous field observation across large tracts with laboratory experiments on heat, pressure, and crystallization to draw robust conclusions about rock transformation processes.
